danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 18
paragraphs: I de seneste to dage, lige siden han forlod sit hjem, havde Pierre boet i det tomme hus, der havde tilhørt hans afdøde velgører, Bazdejev. Det gik til på følgende måde.

Da han vågnede om morgenen efter sin tilbagekomst til Moskva og sit møde med grev Rostoptjin, kunne han i nogen tid ikke begribe, hvor han var, eller hvad der ventedes af ham. Da han blev informeret om, at der blandt andre, der ventede på ham i hans modtagelsesværelse, var en franskmand, som havde bragt et brev fra hans kone, grevinde Hélène, følte han sig pludselig overvældet af den forvirring og håbløshed, som han var tilbøjelig til at bukke under for. Han følte, at alt nu var forbi, at alt var i opløsning og ved at falde fra hinanden, at ingen havde ret eller uret, at fremtiden ikke rummede noget, og at der ikke var nogen udvej. Med et unaturligt smil og mumlende for sig selv satte han sig først på sofaen i en desperat stilling, rejste sig så, gik hen til døren til modtagelsesværelset og kiggede gennem sprækken, vendte tilbage med svingende arme og tog en bog op. Hans hovmester kom ind igen for at sige, at franskmanden, der havde bragt brevet fra grevinden, meget gerne ville tale med ham, bare et minut, og at nogen fra Bazdejevs enke havde spurgt, om Pierre ville tage sig af hendes mands bøger, da hun selv var på vej til landet.
»Åh ja, straks; vent... eller nej! Nej, selvfølgelig... gå og sig, at jeg kommer med det samme,« svarede Pierre til hovmesteren.

Men så snart manden havde forladt værelset, tog Pierre sin hat, der lå på bordet, og gik ud af sit arbejdsværelse ad den anden dør. Der var ingen i gangen. Han gik hele gangen igennem til trappen og gik, rynkende panden og gniende sig i panden med begge hænder, ned til den første afsats. Hallportieren stod ved hoveddøren. Fra afsatsen, hvor Pierre stod, førte en anden trappe ned til bagindgangen. Han gik ned ad den trappe og ud i gården. Ingen havde set ham. Men der holdt nogle vogne, og så snart Pierre trådte ud af porten, lagde kuskene og gårdskarlen mærke til ham og lettede på kasketten. Da han mærkede, at man så på ham, opførte han sig som en struds, der stikker hovedet i en busk for ikke at blive set: han sænkede hovedet, satte farten op og gik ned ad gaden.
Af alle de sager, der ventede Pierre den dag, forekom sorteringen af Josef Bazdejevs bøger og papirer ham den mest nødvendige.
Han hyrede den første droske, han mødte, og bad kusken køre til Patriarkdammene, hvor enken Bazdejevs hus lå.

Mens han ustandseligt vendte sig for at se på rækkerne af læssede vogne, der fra alle sider var på vej ud af Moskva, og balancerede sin store krop for ikke at glide ud af det rystende, gamle køretøj, oplevede Pierre den glade følelse af en dreng, der stikker af fra skolen, og begyndte at tale med kusken.
Manden fortalte ham, at der i dag blev uddelt våben ved Kreml, og at alle i morgen ville blive sendt ud bag Trehjøjsporten, hvor der ville stå et stort slag.

Da Pierre nåede frem til Patriarkdammene, fandt han Bazdejev-familiens hus, som han ikke havde besøgt i lang tid. Han gik hen til porten. Gerasim, den gustne, skægløse gamle mand, som Pierre havde set i Torzjok fem år tidligere sammen med Josef Bazdejev, åbnede døren, da han bankede på.
»Hjemme?« spurgte Pierre.
»På grund af den nuværende tilstand er Sofia Danilovna taget til godset i Torzjok med børnene, Deres excellence.«
»Jeg kommer alligevel ind, jeg skal gennemgå bøgerne,« sagde Pierre.
»Vær så venlig at træde indenfor. Makar Aleksejevitj, min afdøde herres bror — Gud give ham den evige hvile — er blevet her, men han er i en svag tilstand, som De ved,« sagde den gamle tjener.
Pierre vidste, at Makar Aleksejevitj var Josef Bazdejevs halvgale bror og en voldsom dranker.
»Ja, ja, jeg ved det. Lad os gå ind...« sagde Pierre og trådte ind i huset.
En høj, skaldet gammel mand med en rød næse, iført slobrok og med galocher på de bare fødder, stod i forstuen. Da han fik øje på Pierre, mumlede han noget vredt og gik sin vej ned ad gangen.

»Han var en meget klog mand, men er nu blevet ganske svækket, som Deres ære kan se,« sagde Gerasim. »Vil De træde ind i arbejdsværelset?« Pierre nikkede. »Det har været forseglet, og sådan er det blevet, men Sofia Danilovna gav ordre om, at hvis nogen kom fra Dem, skulle de have bøgerne.«
Pierre gik ind i det dystre arbejdsværelse, som han havde bedt ind i med en sådan bæven, dengang hans velgører levede. Rummet, støvet og urørt siden Josef Bazdejevs død, var nu endnu mere dystert.

Gerasim åbnede en af skoderne og forlod værelset på tåspidserne. Pierre gik rundt i værelset, nærmede sig skabet, hvor manuskripterne blev opbevaret, og tog det ud, der engang havde været et af de vigtigste, ordenens allerhelligste. Det var de autentiske skotske ritualer med Bazdejevs noter og forklaringer. Han satte sig ved det støvede skrivebord, lagde manuskripterne foran sig, åbnede dem, lukkede dem, skubbede dem til sidst væk, og med hovedet i hånden hengav han sig til sine tanker.
Gerasim kiggede forsigtigt ind i arbejdsværelset flere gange og så Pierre altid sidde i den samme stilling.
Mere end to timer gik, og Gerasim tillod sig at lave en svag lyd ved døren for at tiltrække hans opmærksomhed, men Pierre hørte ham ikke.
»Skal drosken sendes væk, Deres ære?«

»Åh ja!« sagde Pierre, idet han vågnede op og hastigt rejste sig. »Se her,« tilføjede han, tog Gerasim i en knap i hans frakke og kiggede ned på den gamle mand med fugtige, skinnende og henrevne øjne, »sig mig, ved du, at der kommer et slag i morgen?«
»Det har vi hørt,« svarede manden.
»Jeg beder dig om ikke at fortælle nogen, hvem jeg er, og om at gøre, hvad jeg beder dig om.«
»Ja, Deres excellence,« svarede Gerasim. »Vil De have noget at spise?«
»Nej, men jeg har brug for noget andet. Jeg har brug for bondetøj og en pistol,« sagde Pierre og rødmede uventet.
»Ja, Deres excellence,« sagde Gerasim efter et øjebliks betænkning.

Resten af den dag tilbragte Pierre alene i sin velgørers arbejdsværelse, og Gerasim hørte ham rastløst vandre fra det ene hjørne til det andet og tale med sig selv. Han tilbragte natten på en seng, der var redt til ham dér.

Gerasim, som var en tjener, der i sin tid havde set mange mærkelige ting, accepterede uden overraskelse, at Pierre tog ophold i huset, og syntes glad for at have nogen at varte op. Samme aften — uden overhovedet at spørge sig selv, hvad det skulle bruges til — skaffede han en kuskekappe og kasket til Pierre og lovede at skaffe ham pistolen næste dag. Makar Aleksejevitj kom to gange den aften slæbende i sine galocher hen til døren og standsede og kiggede indsmigrende på Pierre. Men så snart Pierre vendte sig mod ham, svøbte han slobrokken om sig med et flovt og vredt blik og skyndte sig bort. Det var, da Pierre, iført kuskekappe (som Gerasim havde skaffet og desinficeret med damp), var på vej med den gamle mand for at købe pistolen på Sukharev-markedet, at han mødte Rostov-familien.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: For the past two days, since leaving home, Pierre had been living in the empty house of his late benefactor, Bazdeev. This is how it came about.

When he woke up on the morning after his return to Moscow and his meeting with Count Rostopchin, he couldn't at first figure out where he was or what was expected of him. When told that among the people waiting for him in the reception room was a Frenchman who had brought a letter from his wife, Countess Helene, he was suddenly overcome by that feeling of confusion and hopelessness to which he was prone. He felt that everything was finished, everything in chaos, everything crumbling — nobody was right or wrong, the future held nothing, and there was no way out. Smiling awkwardly and muttering to himself, he first sat down on the sofa in a posture of despair, then got up, went to the reception room door, peeked through the crack, came back waving his arms, and picked up a book. His major-domo came in again to say that the Frenchman who'd brought the letter from the countess was very eager to see him, if only for a minute, and that someone from Bazdeev's widow had come asking Pierre to take charge of her late husband's books, as she was leaving for the country.
"Oh, yes — in a moment. Wait... or no! No, of course... go and tell him I'll come directly," Pierre said to the major-domo.

But as soon as the man left, Pierre grabbed his hat from the table and went out of the study through the other door. No one was in the hallway. He walked its full length to the stairs and, frowning and rubbing his forehead with both hands, went down to the first landing. The hall porter was standing at the front door. From the landing where Pierre stood, a second staircase led to the back entrance. He went down it and out into the yard. No one had seen him. But some carriages were waiting, and the moment Pierre stepped through the gate, the coachmen and the yard porter spotted him and raised their caps. Feeling observed, Pierre acted like an ostrich that hides its head in a bush to avoid being seen — he hung his head and, quickening his pace, hurried down the street.
Of all the matters awaiting him that day, sorting through Joseph Bazdeev's books and papers struck Pierre as the most necessary.
He hailed the first cab he found and told the driver to go to the Patriarch's Ponds, where the widow Bazdeev's house was.

Constantly turning around to look at the loaded carts making their way from every direction out of Moscow, and balancing his bulky body so as not to slide out of the rickety old vehicle, Pierre — feeling the joyful relief of a boy escaping school — began chatting with his driver.
The driver told him arms were being distributed at the Kremlin, and that tomorrow everyone would be sent out beyond the Three Hills gates where a great battle would take place.

Having reached the Patriarch's Ponds, Pierre found the Bazdeev house, where he hadn't been in a long time. He went up to the gate. Gerasim — that sallow, beardless old man Pierre had seen at Torzhok five years earlier with Joseph Bazdeev — came out in answer to his knock.
"Is the mistress home?" asked Pierre.
"Due to the present situation, Sophia Danilovna has gone with the children to the Torzhok estate, your excellency."
"I'll come in anyway — I need to look through the books," said Pierre.
"Please, step in. Makar Alexeevich — the brother of my late master, may the kingdom of heaven be his — has stayed here, but he's in a poor state, as you know," said the old servant.
Pierre knew that Makar Alexeevich was Joseph Bazdeev's half-mad brother and a heavy drinker.
"Yes, yes, I know. Let's go in..." Pierre said, and he entered the house.
A tall, bald-headed old man with a red nose, wearing a dressing gown and galoshes on his bare feet, stood in the anteroom. Seeing Pierre, he muttered something angry and shuffled away down the hall.

"He was once a very clever man, but he's grown quite feeble now, as your honor can see," said Gerasim. "Will you come into the study?" Pierre nodded. "It's been kept sealed up just as it was, but Sophia Danilovna gave orders that if anyone came from you, they were to have the books."
Pierre went into the gloomy study he had once entered with such trepidation during his benefactor's lifetime. The room, dusty and untouched since Joseph Bazdeev's death, was gloomier than ever.

Gerasim opened one of the shutters and left the room on tiptoe. Pierre went around the study, approached the cupboard where the manuscripts were kept, and took out what had once been the most sacred treasure of the order — the authentic Scottish Acts with Bazdeev's notes and commentaries. He sat down at the dusty desk, laid the manuscripts before him, opened them, closed them, then pushed them away, and resting his head on his hand, sank into thought.
Gerasim peeked cautiously into the study several times and saw Pierre always sitting in the same position.
More than two hours passed, and Gerasim took the liberty of making a slight noise at the door to get his attention, but Pierre didn't hear him.
"Should the cab be dismissed, your honor?"

"Oh, yes!" said Pierre, rousing himself and jumping up. "Listen," he added, taking Gerasim by a button of his coat and looking down at the old man with moist, shining, ecstatic eyes. "Listen — do you know there's going to be a battle tomorrow?"
"So we've heard," the man replied.
"I beg you not to tell anyone who I am, and to do what I ask."
"Yes, your excellency," Gerasim replied. "Will you have something to eat?"
"No, but I need something else. I need peasant clothes and a pistol," said Pierre, unexpectedly blushing.
"Yes, your excellency," said Gerasim after a moment's thought.
Pierre spent the rest of the day alone in his benefactor's study, and Gerasim heard him pacing restlessly from corner to corner, talking to himself. He spent the night on a bed made up for him there.

Gerasim, as a servant who had seen many strange things in his time, accepted Pierre's taking up residence without surprise and seemed pleased to have someone to wait on. That same evening — without even asking what they were for — he procured a coachman's coat and cap for Pierre and promised to get the pistol the next day. Makar Alexeevich came shuffling in his galoshes to the door twice that evening, stopping to peer ingratiatingly at Pierre. But as soon as Pierre turned toward him, he wrapped his dressing gown around himself with a shamefaced, angry look and hurried away. It was when Pierre — wearing the coachman's coat Gerasim had obtained and disinfected by steaming — was on his way with the old man to buy the pistol at the Sukharev market that he encountered the Rostovs.
